Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "can you turn these notes into a clear exhibit brief for Harbor Steps Museum, and send the brief to Leonie, not Ellis. The exhibit is called “The Sound of the Tide Bell.” It is about the North Quay tide bell, the people who maintained it and the memories local residents associate with it. Please keep the brief grounded in the notes below, including the interview excerpts and the source details; don’t write the exhibit itself or fill in gaps with guesses. The museum’s temporary exhibition opens 12 September 2026 and closes 30 November 2026. It will be in Gallery 2, admission is free, and the gallery has four display cases and one audio station. The request is for an exhibit brief, not a press release or a visitor leaflet. Make it clear what the exhibit is about and what material is available, without suggesting that every source will necessarily be displayed.

Some background notes from the museum file: the bell was installed at North Quay in 1912 and was sounded as a fog warning until 1978. The surviving bell is now held by the town archive and is being lent to the museum for this exhibition. The archive’s inventory calls it “North Quay fog bell,” while the proposed exhibit title is “The Sound of the Tide Bell”; retain both names in their respective contexts rather than silently replacing one with the other. The notes say the bell was sounded by hand, but they do not give a regular schedule or say how often it rang. The brief should not claim a particular number of rings, a daily routine, or that the bell was used for any other purpose. The museum wants the maintenance work and local recollections to be visible alongside the object’s history, rather than presenting the bell only as an old piece of equipment.

The research folder includes a 1912 installation ledger, two maintenance entries, a 1978 harbour notice, and interviews recorded by museum staff in 2025. The ledger records delivery of the bell to North Quay in April 1912 and installation in May of that year; it does not name the workers who installed it. A maintenance entry dated 1936 says that the clapper pin was replaced. Another, dated 1954, records inspection of the mounting bracket and tightening of two bolts. Neither entry identifies the person who did the work. The harbour notice, dated 3 October 1978, says the fog bell service would end on 15 October 1978, with a radio warning service taking its place. Do not turn that into a claim that the bell was removed on that date: the notes give no removal date. The source folder is held by the Harbor Steps Museum archive, reference HS-NTQ-14.

Interview excerpts, recorded 4 May 2025 with retired dock worker Mara Venn: “My father showed me where the rope ran, but by then nobody was using it for warnings. He said you had to keep the hinge clear of salt.” Venn worked at North Quay from 1968 to 1991. The interview notes say that she remembered helping to clear debris near the bell housing as a teenager; they do not say she operated the bell. A second excerpt from the same interview is: “When the fog came right up to the sheds, you could hear the harbor change. The bell was one sound among several, not the whole story.” Keep her words as an interview quotation if quoted, and don’t make her speak for everyone who worked at the quay.

Interview excerpts, recorded 12 May 2025 with local resident Ivo Chen, whose family lived near the quay from 1972 to 2003: “I knew the bell was there before I knew what it was for. In winter the sound carried across our street, though I can’t tell you how often it rang.” Chen said his grandmother called it “the old warning,” but the interview notes do not identify which years she used that phrase. A later excerpt reads: “After the radio notices started, people still pointed out the bell when they walked past. It didn’t vanish from the neighborhood just because it wasn’t being sounded.” The brief can use these as separate recollections, but shouldn’t present either one as a verified account of the bell’s operating schedule or imply that Chen’s family owned or maintained it.

There are also two short staff source notes. Collections assistant Nadiya Sato checked the archive inventory on 18 February 2026 and confirmed that the bell is listed there under “North Quay fog bell.” The loan record says the object is expected to be available for the exhibition, but the installation plan has not yet been approved. Do not describe the display arrangement as settled. The second note is from oral history coordinator Peter Vale, who says the interview recordings are retained by the museum and that the excerpts above were selected for preliminary planning. The notes do not state whether the full interviews will be played at the audio station, or whether any audio will be used at all.

Please make the brief useful to the museum team by organizing the material into a short overview, a section on the documentary and object sources, and a section on what the two interviews contribute. A numbered section is fine if it helps. Include the exhibition name, dates, location, free admission, and the available gallery features. Keep source attribution and dates clear, distinguish recorded information from interview memory, and retain the quoted wording accurately. Don’t invent a curator, a visitor activity, an installation design, a confirmed audio plan, or additional historical claims. End with the practical note that the installation plan has not yet been approved and that the source notes do not specify whether interview audio will be used; keep those as separate facts, not a conclusion about what the museum should do.", "output": "Please prepare an exhibit brief for Harbor Steps Museum and send it to Leonie, not Ellis. The brief should cover the temporary exhibition “The Sound of the Tide Bell.” Keep it grounded in the information below, including the interview excerpts and source details. Do not write the exhibit itself, fill gaps with guesses, or imply that every available source will be displayed. This is an exhibit brief, not a press release or visitor leaflet. Explain the subject and the material available.

The exhibition opens 12 September 2026 and closes 30 November 2026. It will be in Gallery 2, admission is free, and the gallery has four display cases and one audio station. The exhibition concerns the North Quay tide bell, the people who maintained it, and local residents’ memories of it. The museum wants the maintenance work and recollections to appear alongside the object’s history, rather than presenting the bell only as an old piece of equipment.

1. Background and documentary sources

The bell was installed at North Quay in 1912 and sounded as a fog warning until 1978. The surviving bell is held by the town archive and is being lent to the museum for this exhibition. The archive inventory calls it “North Quay fog bell”; the proposed exhibition title is “The Sound of the Tide Bell.” Keep each name in its stated context. The notes say the bell was sounded by hand, but do not give a regular schedule or say how often it rang. Do not claim a particular number of rings, a daily routine, or any other use.

The research folder contains a 1912 installation ledger, two maintenance entries, a 1978 harbour notice, and interviews recorded by museum staff in 2025. The ledger records delivery of the bell to North Quay in April 1912 and installation in May. It does not name the workers who installed it. A 1936 maintenance entry records replacement of the clapper pin. An entry from 1954 records inspection of the mounting bracket and tightening of two bolts. Neither entry identifies who did the work. The harbour notice, dated 3 October 1978, says the fog bell service would end on 15 October 1978, with a radio warning service taking its place. The notes give no removal date, so do not say the bell was removed on 15 October. The source folder is held by the Harbor Steps Museum archive, reference HS-NTQ-14.

2. Interview material

Mara Venn’s interview was recorded on 4 May 2025. Venn is a retired dock worker who worked at North Quay from 1968 to 1991. She recalled: “My father showed me where the rope ran, but by then nobody was using it for warnings. He said you had to keep the hinge clear of salt.” The interview notes say she remembered helping to clear debris near the bell housing as a teenager; they do not say she operated the bell. A second excerpt is: “When the fog came right up to the sheds, you could hear the harbor change. The bell was one sound among several, not the whole story.” If quoted, retain her words accurately. Do not make Venn speak for everyone who worked at the quay.

Ivo Chen’s interview was recorded on 12 May 2025. His family lived near the quay from 1972 to 2003. Chen said: “I knew the bell was there before I knew what it was for. In winter the sound carried across our street, though I can’t tell you how often it rang.” He said his grandmother called it “the old warning,” but the interview notes do not identify the years in which she used that phrase. A later excerpt reads: “After the radio notices started, people still pointed out the bell when they walked past. It didn’t vanish from the neighborhood just because it wasn’t being sounded.” These are separate recollections, not verified evidence of an operating schedule. Do not imply that Chen’s family owned or maintained the bell.

3. Staff notes and status

Collections assistant Nadiya Sato checked the archive inventory on 18 February 2026 and confirmed that the bell is listed as “North Quay fog bell.” The loan record says the object is expected to be available for the exhibition, but the installation plan has not yet been approved. Do not describe the display arrangement as settled. Oral history coordinator Peter Vale notes that the interview recordings are retained by the museum and that the excerpts above were selected for preliminary planning. The notes do not say whether the full interviews will be played at the audio station or whether any audio will be used.

Keep source attribution and dates clear, and distinguish recorded information from interview memory. Include the exhibition name, dates, location, free admission, and available gallery features. Do not invent a curator, visitor activity, installation design, confirmed audio plan, or additional historical claims. End with these two separate practical facts: the installation plan has not yet been approved; the source notes do not specify whether interview audio will be used."}]
